To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the consumption of carbohydrates (whole grain bread, breakfast cereals, oats/oatmeal, root vegetables, green leafy vegetables, cooked vegetables and cruciferous vegetable), nuts (all nuts, tree nuts and peanuts) and fish was associated with a reduction in all-cause and cardiovascular mortality.

the highest level of scientific evidence suggests that whole grain bread, breakfast cereal, oats/oatmeal, fish, nuts, vegetables, and fruit (with the exception of tinned fruit) are beneficial for cardiovascular health.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of dietary patterns in the development of cardiovascular disease.
the role that diet and lifestyle play in the development of chronic diseases.
the effects of diet and lifestyle on the development of cardiovascular disease and the prevention of atherosclerosis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the optimal diet to reduce cardiovascular disease risk is a diet high in carbohydrates and vegetables, with a high intake of fish and nuts, but low in processed meat and tanned fruit.
the Mediterranean diet is associated with reduced risk of cardiovascular disease, and that this diet should be recommended for all individuals.
a diet rich in whole grains, fish and vegetables is beneficial, while a diet rich in red meat and processed meats is harmful.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a diet rich in whole grains, vegetables, fruits, nuts and fish and low in red meat and processed meats is associated with the lowest mortality.
a healthy diet is a diet that is low in processed meat and tined fruit, and high in whole grains, fish and vegetables.
a diet high in plant-based foods and low in animal-based foods is likely to have cardiovascular and health benefits.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the optimal diet for cardiovascular disease and all cause mortality is a healthy diet that is low in processed foods, high in whole foods and high in vegetables.
there are many dietary components with strong and consistent evidence for benefit, which may provide a more useful approach for clinicians and patients than a single dietary pattern.
a healthy diet is not just about what you eat, it is also about what you don't eat.
